newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian parliament to convene on July 28.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian parliament to convene on July 28.

text.p: Cambodian members of parliament on Monday formally agreed to convene the National Assembly on July 28, when they are expected to name a replacement for the country's ousted premier under unusually heavy security.
The members stopped short of putting the candidacy of Foreign Minister Ung Huot on the formal agenda, however.

Ung Huot, who has been tipped to replace ousted First Prime Minister Norodom Ranariddh, had not yet been approved by Ranariddh's royalist FUNCINPEC party, the members said after a meeting of the assembly's powerful permanent committee.

"We haven't gotten the documents for the appointment for the new prime minister yet, but if they come on time, we will put the matter at the top of our agenda," said Deputy Secretary General Chan Ven.

He did not provide details on when FUNCINPEC would approve the candidate, but analysts said the party's approval could take several days as it attempted to reorganise its rosters and assess how many members were left in the country.
Members of parliament are still picking up the pieces of the country's broken government since Second Prime Minister Hun Sen ousted Ranariddh in a July 6 coup.
In the wake of the violent overthrow of Ranariddh, dozens of his loyalists, including about 20 members of parliament, left the country.
Among those royalists who stayed, 40 are believed to have been killed.
Chan Ven said parliament was asking members of FUNCINPEC who fled to come back to the country, and extra security measures would be implemented for the parliament session.
"We are requiring strong security at our session," he said. "It's the first such measure of its kind because we are afraid about our personal security."
Nearly half of the permanent committee's 12 members were still out of the country on Monday.

Most seats were filled voluntarily by deputies of the departed royalist sympathisers in what analysts said was a sign the new regime would do whatever was necessary to replace Ranariddh's loyalists and keep the government moving.
Analysts said the 120-member National Assembly, scheduled to convene on July 28, would also likely make a quorum of 84 members.

A bigger challenge than filling seats would be convincing the outside world that the body -- which is three months overdue in meeting -- is still democratic, they said. The assembly was due to have met in April but the date was postponed as a result of the simmering tension between Hun Sen and Ranariddh.
Hun Sen has courted world favour for his new regime by promising he would replace Ranariddh and keep the constitution, parliament and monarchy functioning.
U.S. President Bill Clinton's special envoy on Cambodia, Stephen Solarz, was reported to have said on Monday that Washington would not recognise Ung Huot as Ranariddh's replacement.
Kyodo News Service said Solarz made the comment in a meeting in Tokyo with Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda.
He said the United States was concerned the decision would not be an expression of the assembly's free will because a number of its legislators would not be present, Kyodo reported.
